reference.source: Kelley and Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology
clinicalPearls: Drug-induced vasculitis most often manifests as a small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis with palpable purpura on dependent areas, typically days to weeks after starting the culprit drug.
A distinct drug-induced ANCA-associated vasculitis is well recognised, classically with antimyeloperoxidase antibodies, and can affect the kidneys and lungs.
Antithyroid drugs, hydralazine, minocycline, certain anti-tumour necrosis factor agents and cocaine adulterated with levamisole are among the well-described triggers.
Very high-titre antimyeloperoxidase antibodies, antibodies to multiple antigens, or combined MPO and PR3 positivity should raise suspicion of a drug cause.
Withdrawal of the offending agent is the cornerstone of management and often leads to resolution of milder cutaneous disease.
Severe organ-threatening disease (glomerulonephritis, alveolar haemorrhage) may still require immunosuppression despite drug cessation.
Levamisole-adulterated cocaine characteristically causes retiform purpura with ear involvement, neutropenia and positive ANCA.
A detailed drug and substance history, including over-the-counter agents and illicit drugs, is essential to identify the trigger.
reference.pathophysiology: Drug-induced vasculitis arises when a drug or its metabolites trigger an immune-mediated attack on blood vessel walls. In hypersensitivity small-vessel vasculitis the drug acts as a hapten, driving immune-complex formation and deposition in postcapillary venules with complement activation and neutrophil-mediated leukocytoclastic injury. In drug-induced ANCA-associated vasculitis certain agents promote the generation of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, often against myeloperoxidase; some drugs are thought to alter neutrophil extracellular trap formation or unmask sequestered antigens, breaking tolerance. The result ranges from purely cutaneous disease to a necrotising small-vessel vasculitis with renal and pulmonary involvement indistinguishable from idiopathic disease.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed drug, over-the-counter and illicit substance history including timeline
ANCA testing with antigen specificity (MPO and PR3), noting high titres or dual positivity
Renal function and urinalysis to detect glomerulonephritis
Full blood count looking for neutropenia (as with levamisole)
Complement, cryoglobulins and infection screen to exclude alternatives
Urine toxicology where illicit drug exposure is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine
Extensive retiform purpura with skin necrosis
Systemic features persisting despite drug withdrawal
reference.prognosis: Cutaneous-limited disease usually resolves after the culprit drug is stopped, but organ-threatening ANCA-associated forms can cause lasting renal impairment if not treated promptly. Rechallenge with the offending agent risks recurrence and should be avoided.
pitfalls: Failing to take a complete drug and substance history, including illicit drugs and supplements.
Not recognising drug-induced ANCA vasculitis and treating it as idiopathic while continuing the trigger.
Missing levamisole-adulterated cocaine as a cause of retiform purpura with neutropenia.
Assuming all drug-induced vasculitis is benign and self-limiting when severe organ involvement can occur.
Rechallenging the patient with the causative drug, precipitating relapse.

management: Identify and permanently withdraw the culprit agent (for example antithyroid drugs, hydralazine, minocycline, anti-tumour necrosis factor agents or levamisole-adulterated cocaine) as the cornerstone of treatment
For milder cutaneous leukocytoclastic disease, provide supportive care with leg elevation, wound care for purpura and analgesia while awaiting resolution after drug cessation
Treat organ-threatening ANCA-associated disease (glomerulonephritis or alveolar haemorrhage) with corticosteroids plus a further immunosuppressive agent such as cyclophosphamide or rituximab
Reserve plasma exchange for severe pulmonary haemorrhage or rapidly progressive renal failure
Monitor renal function and urinalysis for evolving glomerulonephritis and check the full blood count for drug-induced neutropenia
Refer promptly to rheumatology and nephrology for confirmation, biopsy and immunosuppression decisions
Document the reaction clearly and avoid rechallenge with the offending drug, which risks recurrence
